title: 6.3 Correlated Assets
bodyHtml:
6.3 Correlated Assets

Why This Matters

Beginners often think:

different charts mean different risk

That is not always true.

You can hold three positions in three different markets and still be making one big bet on the same macro idea.

That is why correlation matters. It helps you see when your trades are connected, even if the symbols look different.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • define correlation in simple language;
  • identify when several positions may carry hidden overlap;
  • use correlation as context for risk management instead of as a prediction machine.

What Correlation Means

Correlation is a way of describing how two assets often move in relation to each other.

Type Plain-English meaning Simple example
Positive correlation Two assets often move in the same direction Two equity indices rising together during a broad risk-on move
Negative correlation Two assets often move in opposite directions The U.S. dollar rising while EUR/USD falls
Changing correlation The relationship is not stable all the time Gold and yields may move differently when the market focus changes

(Table alt-text: A three-row table explaining positive, negative, and changing correlation with simple examples.)

The most important rule is this:

correlation is a tendency, not a promise

If a relationship worked last month, that does not guarantee it will work the same way next week.

Why the U.S. Dollar Connects So Many Charts

The dollar matters because it sits in the middle of many global trades.

The BIS 2025 Triennial Survey says the U.S. dollar was on one side of 89.2% of all FX trades in April 2025. The same BIS release says the top 10 most traded currency pairs all involved the U.S. dollar.

That helps explain why a strong dollar move can affect many charts at once, including:

  • EUR/USD;
  • GBP/USD;
  • gold;
  • some equity indices;
  • some commodity-linked currencies.

The ICE U.S. Dollar Index page also describes the dollar index as a benchmark that tracks the value of the dollar against a basket of world currencies.

Hidden Double Risk

Look at these examples:

Positions What they may really express Hidden risk
Long EUR/USD and long GBP/USD A weaker U.S. dollar view A stronger dollar can hurt both trades together
Long S&P 500 and long Nasdaq A broad equity risk-on view One macro shock can hit both indices
Long gold, long EUR/USD, and long AUD/USD A softer-dollar or easier-policy theme Three charts can lose together from one dollar surge
Long Brent crude and long an energy-sector ETF A higher-oil or tighter-supply theme One oil reversal can hit both the commodity and the stock exposure

(Table alt-text: A four-row table showing how different positions can still express the same macro theme and create overlapping risk across FX, stock indices, metals, and energy.)

This is a practical form of concentration risk.

FINRA explains concentration risk as the danger of amplified losses when too much exposure is tied to one investment, asset class, market segment, or correlated group of positions.

For a trader, the idea is simple:

if one news event can damage all my positions at once, I may not be diversified at all

Correlation Helps With Context, Not Certainty

Correlation can help you ask better questions:

  • Are my trades linked to the same macro story?
  • Would one surprise event hit several positions together?
  • Am I spreading risk, or just repeating it?

What correlation cannot do:

  • guarantee that one chart must copy another;
  • replace chart structure;
  • replace a stop, position size, or risk plan.

If a single stock falls while the index rises, that does not mean the market is broken. It may simply mean that company has its own story.

One Simple Example

Imagine you are holding:

  1. long EUR/USD;
  2. long GBP/USD;
  3. long gold.

At first, this feels diversified because you are in FX and commodities.

But ask the deeper question:

What happens if the U.S. dollar suddenly strengthens?

A stronger dollar could pressure:

  • EUR/USD lower;
  • GBP/USD lower;
  • gold lower.

You did not spread your risk across three different ideas. You repeated one idea three times.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Counting Symbols Instead of Themes

Three positions are not diversified if they all depend on the same macro move.

Mistake 2: Treating Correlation as Permanent

Relationships can weaken, flip, or disappear.

Mistake 3: Using Correlation Instead of Price Structure

Context helps, but the chart still needs its own trade plan.

Mistake 4: Ignoring Position Overlap During Event Weeks

Macro events can hit several related markets at once.
learningOutcomes: explain correlation as a tendency rather than a permanent rule;
identify when multiple positions may carry hidden overlap;
use cross-asset relationships for context instead of certainty.

quizItems.prompt: What is the best beginner definition of correlation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A permanent law that never changes

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tendency for assets to move in related ways over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: A guarantee that one asset predicts another

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: A tendency for assets to move in related ways over time

quizItems.explanation: The lesson teaches correlation as a changing relationship, not a fixed law.

quizItems.prompt: Why can three different positions still be one large risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because different symbols can still express the same macro theme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because every market always moves randomly

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because diversification only works in crypto

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because risk disappears when trades are opened in separate tabs

correctAnswer.label: A
correctAnswer.text: Because different symbols can still express the same macro theme

quizItems.explanation: The hidden-overlap section shows how multiple trades can repeat one idea.

quizItems.prompt: What is the disciplined use of correlation in this course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use it as context for risk overlap and confirmation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Assume one market must always copy another

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replace price structure with correlation guesses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Remove stops when markets usually move together

correctAnswer.label: A
correctAnswer.text: Use it as context for risk overlap and confirmation
